chunks.content: CS301 Database Management Systems is a 4-credit course offered in the fifth semester. Prerequisites: CS201 Data Structures and Algorithms. The course meets twice weekly for 90-minute lectures and includes a weekly two-hour laboratory session.

Assessment weighting: continuous assessment 40% (two quizzes worth 10% each and one project worth 20%), mid-semester examination 20%, and final examination 40%. A minimum of 40% in the final examination is required to pass the course.

Attendance policy: students must attend at least 75% of lectures and laboratory sessions to be eligible for the final examination. Medical absences must be documented within one week of returning to class.

Learning outcomes: by the end of the course students will be able to explain relational concepts, write SQL queries, apply normalization, analyze transaction management and evaluate indexing strategies. Recommended textbook: Silberschatz, Korth and Sudarshan, Database System Concepts, 7th edition.
A functional dependency X -> Y holds in a relation when every pair of tuples that agree on X also agree on Y. Functional dependencies are the formal basis for normalization.

A relation is in second normal form (2NF) if it is in first normal form and every non-prime attribute is fully functionally dependent on every candidate key; that is, there are no partial dependencies.

A relation is in third normal form (3NF) if it is in 2NF and no non-prime attribute is transitively dependent on a candidate key. Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is stricter: for every non-trivial dependency X -> Y, X must be a superkey.

Decomposition into BCNF is always lossless-join but may not be dependency-preserving. When dependency preservation is essential, designers often settle for 3NF, which guarantees both lossless join and dependency preservation.
First-Come First-Served (FCFS) scheduling runs processes in arrival order. It is simple but suffers from the convoy effect, where short processes wait behind a long one.

Shortest Job First (SJF) selects the process with the smallest next CPU burst and is provably optimal for minimizing average waiting time, but it requires knowledge of future burst lengths, which is usually estimated with exponential averaging of previous bursts.

Round-robin scheduling gives each process a fixed time quantum. A very small quantum increases context-switch overhead, whereas a very large quantum degenerates into FCFS. A quantum of 10 to 100 milliseconds is typical.
Multilevel feedback queues allow processes to move between queues based on their observed CPU usage, favouring interactive processes while still guaranteeing progress for long-running jobs.

documents.document_name: Department Grading and Academic Integrity Policy.pdf

chunks.content: Grades are assigned on a ten-point scale: O (90-100), A+ (80-89), A (70-79), B+ (60-69), B (50-59), C (40-49) and F (below 40). Grade moderation is performed by a departmental committee before results are published.

Requests for re-evaluation of a final examination script must be submitted within seven working days of the publication of results together with the prescribed fee. Re-evaluation is performed by a different examiner.

Plagiarism, including the unattributed use of generated text, is an academic integrity violation. A first offence results in zero marks for the assessment; a second offence is referred to the disciplinary committee.
